title: TA8-07274
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX citizens of Mexico, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA).1
The claimants' identities have been established through certified copies of the claimants' passports found in Exhibit R/A-2.2 ALLEGATIONS
The claimants, who are brothers, allege fear of harm at the hands of an individual known as XXXXX, a member of the Los Zetas (Zetas), a criminal organization.

XXXXX was employed as a police officer from XXXXX 2001 to XXXXX 2006. In the XXXXX of 2001, during the course of his duties as a XXXXX, XXXXX prevented a vehicle of the Zetas gang members from entering an area that was cordoned off for an XXXXX. This angered the gang members and their leader known as XXXXX. Two months later XXXXX received a phone call at the police station from XXXXX. He was demanding that the police release a vehicle being searched. When XXXXX request was denied, he and other gang members went to the police station to see who had denied their request. XXXXX recognized XXXXX from the first incident and told XXXXX that he was going to kill him. In XXXXX 2006, XXXXX received information from an informant that XXXXX, having just returned from southern Mexico, wanted XXXXX dead. In XXXXX 2006, XXXXX, also a police officer, was abducted by cartel members who physically assaulted and threatened him. The cartel members questioned XXXXX about XXXXX whereabouts and XXXXX involvement with XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. XXXXX and XXXXX quit their jobs as police officers following the abduction and went into hiding. They fled to Canada on XXXXX 2007 and filed for refugee protection on June 15, 2007.

I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. The claimants do not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason and their removal to Mexico would not subject them personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.
The determinative issues are that there is an internal flight alternative (IFA) to Mexico City and that there is adequate state protection in Mexico. ANALYSIS Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

The determinative issue in this analysis is whether there is an IFA in the claimant's country of origin, where there is no serious possibility of the claimants being persecuted and where the claimants could safely live without facing a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.

In assessing whether a viable IFA exists, the Board is guided by the cases of the Federal Court of Appeal. If there is a safe haven for claimants in their own country, where they could live free from harm, they are expected to avail themselves of it before they seek safety in Canada, unless they can show it is objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for them to do so.3 The IFA must be realistic, attainable and accessible. Barriers to getting to the IFA must be reasonably surmountable and the claimant cannot be required to encounter great danger or undergo undue hardship either in travelling there or in remaining there. A claimant cannot reject an IFA for frivolous reasons such as not liking the weather there, having no friends or family in the region or not being able to find suitable work there. The fact that a claimant may be better off in Canada economically, physically or emotionally, than they would be in their own country, is not a factor to consider when assessing the reasonableness of an IFA.4 If a viable IFA exists, a claimant is not then a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

In order to determine whether a viable IFA exists, the Board must consider a two-pronged test: 1. The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted, or in this case, that the claimant would not be subject personally to a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture, in the part of the country to which it finds an internal flight alternative exists; and 2. Conditions in that part of the country must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for the claimant to seek refuge there.5

The claimant always bears the burden of proof to show that they would be subject personally, on a balance of probabilities,6 to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the entire country and specifically in the potential IFA area named.7
In this case, the claimants allege fear of XXXXX, a Zetas member.

XXXXX was asked if they could reside in Mexico City so as to avoid XXXXX. He testified that they could not live in Mexico City because the cartel operates in all of Mexico. He also indicated that many cartel supporters have infiltrated the Mexican authorities and that they would not be able to get protection there.
I have considered the evidence, and notwithstanding the testimony of the claimant, I determine that there is an IFA for the claimant in Mexico City.

The Federal District is the largest city in the country and one of many that made serious efforts to address crime and corruption. Mexico has a population of 110 million8 and is close to two million square kilometres in size. Mexico City has a population of 8.8 million people.9 Twenty-two million people live in the Federal District and adjacent urban areas. Every year, the population of the state of Mexico increases by 350,000 people, and 58 per cent of the inhabitants come from poor regions and are [translation] "drawn by the economic dream".10 A 2005 United Nations (UN) Human Development report indicated the differences in the quality of life in Mexico: According to the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) report, certain areas of "Mexico City and the industrial hub of Monterrey in the north could be compared to rich European cities, but other parts of the capital and rural areas in the south of the country" are much poorer (26 Oct. 2004).11

The Board must consider whether the agents of persecution are motivated or likely to pursue the claimants to Mexico City and if they would have the means to do so. XXXXX testified that he believes that he and XXXXX are on the cartel's list of persons the cartel needs to deal with. I find that the agent of persecution is unlikely to pursue the claimants to Mexico City. XXXXX did not pursue the claimants when the claimants were in XXXXX in the northern state of XXXXX and XXXXX was in a southern state. Moreover, there is no persuasive evidence that he would be able to locate the claimants in Mexico City, even if he were so inclined. There is no documentary evidence to indicate individuals could use contacts in the government or bribe government authorities to access private information or the address of an individual. Rather, the documentary evidence states that: Regarding whether the police, government authorities or individuals can use the Voter Registration Card to access information in the official computer system in order to locate an individual within Mexico, the IEEM official noted that, according to Article 135 of the Federal Code of Institutions and Electoral Procedures, documents, data and information provided by Mexican citizens to the Federal Registry of Voters is strictly confidential and cannot be divulged to anyone except authorized users within the organization (Mexico 12 May 2006). No reports of police, government authorities or individuals using the Voter Registration Card to access the information in the official computer system in order to locate an individual within Mexico could be found among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate.12

Therefore, the claimants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a serious possibility of being persecuted or that they would be subjected personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture in Mexico City by XXXXX.
XXXXX was asked if state protection would be available to them in Mexico City. He replied that it would not be because every single level of the police and military is corrupt.

Even if they were to need state protection in Mexico City, I find that there is adequate state protection for victims of crime there. Notwithstanding the testimony of XXXXX, which I found to be unsubstantiated, regarding his views concerning state protection in Mexico City, it is not corroborated by country condition documents. Rather, having canvassed the country conditions documents,13 I find that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. There is nothing in the documentary evidence before the Board to suggest that Mexico is in a state of complete breakdown. There is information before the Board which suggests that criminality and corruption continue to exist in all of Mexico and Mexico City is no exception to this. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists.

The Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical, and a complainant can seek redress at a higher level if dissatisfied with the services at the local level. According to the documentary evidence14, there are a number of authorities and agencies who will assist members of the public if they believe they have encountered a corrupt official or if they are not satisfied with the services of the security forces.

There is documentary evidence15 that persons who face police misconduct, inefficiency or corruption can ask the Secretariat of the Public Administration (SFP), the Program Against Impunity, or the Office of the Attorney General (PGR) to investigate federal and state police failures or misconduct.

Further documentary evidence16 indicates that persons seeking redress from corrupt or complicit officials can do so through the National or State Human Rights Commissions and the General Comptroller's Assistance Directorate.

It is noted that transgressors on the security forces face sanctions, removal, suspension or dismissal.17 In addition, the Federal Agency of Investigation (AFI) deals with corrupt state officials, drug traffickers and kidnappers.

Documentary evidence18 indicates that efforts to ensure police effectiveness and purge corruption include investigations by the Secretary of Public Security, complaints monitored by the Inspector General, and a 24-hour hot line to report corrupt officials.

Further documentary evidence19 indicates that the security forces have instituted new recruiting procedures, drug testing, economic incentives, education and certification of officers, with sanctions levied against ineffective or corrupt officers, including arrests, prosecutions and convictions of members of the security forces. The new government laws attacking corruption and bribery have resulted in sentences of five to 10 years' imprisonment for convicted officials, which have reportedly had a marked effect.20

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available.21 To rebut this presumption, the claimant must provide clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its nationals.22 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.23

No state is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times and the fact that the state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.24

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy in that state. In a democracy such as Mexico, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful.25 The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action reasonably available to them.26 Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.27

I found the claimant's responses regarding the effectiveness of state protection were largely speculative. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in Mexico City for victims of crime, and that generally, Mexico is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. I find that the claimants have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of Mexico, including Mexico City, would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimants seek it.

Furthermore, the Board does not find it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to expect either of the claimants to move to Mexico City, before seeking refugee status in Canada. The claimants each have over 10 years of education, both have worked in law enforcement for a number of years and both have skills in the XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX from working in the family businesses. Having considered the education and employment history of each of the claimants, I am satisfied neither of these factors would create an unduly harsh situation for either the claimants.28

I conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, there is no serious possibility of the claimants being persecuted and would not face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Mexico City at the hands of Balderas. Further, I am satisfied that it would not be unreasonable, in all of the circumstances, including those particular to the claimants, for the claimants to seek refuge in Mexico City.

I determine that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
